facts.statement: Gansus was first described in 1984 based on a single isolated left leg fossil.
facts.quote: It was first described in 1984 on the basis of an isolated left leg.

facts.statement: The initial discovery of Gansus occurred in 1981 when a single fossil foot was found.
facts.quote: Gansus was discovered in the form of a single fossil foot in 1981.

facts.statement: Five additional well-preserved fossils were discovered between 2003 and 2004 in mudstone at an ancient lake site in Changma, Gansu.
facts.quote: Five more well-preserved fossils were found in 2003–2004 in mudstone at the site of an ancient lake at Changma, Gansu

facts.statement: Gansus was approximately the size of a pigeon and resembled loons and diving ducks in appearance.
facts.quote: It was about the size of a pigeon and similar in appearance to loons and diving ducks.

facts.statement: While sharing many features with modern birds, Gansus retained primitive traits including claws on its wings.
facts.quote: It had many features common among modern birds, and also retained some basal traits such as its clawed wings.

facts.statement: Exceptional preservation in anoxic mud allowed fossils to retain flight feathers and toe webbing.
facts.quote: these specimens preserved remains of flight feathers and traces of the webbing between their toes.

facts.statement: Research suggests Gansus was capable of both flight and diving, potentially using its wings, feet, or both for underwater locomotion.
facts.quote: Nudds et al. (2013) showed that the pectoral limb length proportions of Gansus were most similar to swifts and hummingbirds (Apodiformes), while the pelvic limb length proportions fell within the modern birds (Neornithes), showing similarities with grebes (Podicipedidae), albatross (Diomedeidae) and cormorants (Phalacrocoracidae), suggesting that Gansus was both volant and capable of diving to some degree using either foot-propelled or, perhaps, both its wings and its feet for underwater locomotion.

facts.statement: Gansus was an aquatic bird that lived during the Early Cretaceous in what is now western China.
facts.quote: Gansus is a genus of aquatic avialans that lived during the Aptian age of the Early Cretaceous (Aptian-Albian) period in what are now Gansu and Liaoning provinces, western China.

facts.statement: Fossils of Gansus date to approximately 120 million years ago.
facts.quote: The rock layers from which their fossils have been recovered are dated to 120 million years ago.

facts.statement: Gansus is recognized as the oldest known member of the Ornithurae clade, which includes modern birds and extinct relatives like Ichthyornis.
facts.quote: It is the oldest-known member of the Ornithurae, the group which includes modern birds (Neornithes) and extinct related groups, such as Ichthyornis and Hesperornithes.

facts.statement: There is a scientific debate regarding whether the species G. zheni is distinct or a synonym of Iteravis huchzermeyeri.
facts.quote: In 2014, new species G. zheni is described, but some researchers consider this species to be a synonym of Iteravis huchzermeyeri.

facts.statement: A 2026 study described a cluster of bones possibly belonging to Gansus found inside a pellet produced by a non-avian theropod.
facts.quote: A cluster of bones of an ornithuromorph bird (possibly Gansus), interpreted as most likely to be originally contained within a pellet produced by a non-avian theropod (possibly Jian changmaensis), is described from the Lower Cretaceous strata of the Xiagou Formation (China) by Wang et al. (2026).

rejected.statement: Scientists hypothesize that all modern birds may have descended specifically from a semi-aquatic bird similar to Gansus.
rejected.quote: It is now thought possible that all modern birds descended specifically from a semi-aquatic bird similar to Gansus.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'descended specifically from a semi-aquatic bird similar to'
